name: 3rd Sunday of Advent
description: Gaudete Sunday, the joyous Sunday in the middle of Advent.
biblicalBasis: John sends word from prison: "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" Jesus answers by pointing to the signs: "The blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them" (Matt 11:2-6, Luke 7:18-23). Jesus' testimony about John: "Among those born of women there has arisen no one greater."
significance: Joy breaks through in the midst of waiting and preparation. Jesus' answer to John shows that the Messiah did not come as a political conqueror, but as a healer and liberator. The signs he points to are the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecies — God's kingdom breaks in through mercy, not power.
liturgicalContext: Called "Gaudete" after the introit from Phil 4:4: "Rejoice in the Lord always!" Some traditions use the liturgical color rose on this Sunday instead of purple, and the third Advent candle may be rose. A joyful interruption in the solemnity of Advent.
history: The Gaudete tradition dates back to the Middle Ages. The rose candle symbolizes a relaxation of fasting. In Rome, it was customary for the pope to bless a golden rose on this Sunday.
otConnections: Isaiah 35:1-10 — the wilderness shall rejoice and blossom; the holy way is opened. Isaiah 61:1-3 concerning the anointing of the Lord's Spirit: to preach good news to the poor, to bind up those who have a broken heart. Zephaniah 3:14-17: "The Lord your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save."

references.reason: The entire pericope (Matt 11:1-30) is the liturgical text for the 3rd Sunday of Advent (Gaudete). The text begins with John's question and Jesus' answer about the signs (vv. 2-6), continues with Jesus' testimony about John (vv. 7-15), the parable of the unresponsive generation (vv. 16-19), the rebuke of the unrepentant cities (vv. 20-24), and concludes with Jesus' invitation to rest (vv. 25-30). All these parts belong together in a coherent proclamation about recognizing the Messiah and receiving him. There is no reason to split up the text or associate it primarily with St. John's Day in this context.
